1.title: Thinking, Caching, Batch, Platforms and API Errors
1.text: Welcome to Module three: Thinking, Caching, Batch, Platforms and A P I Errors. This module covers the skills claude a p i mechanics, part two: thinking, caching, invoking claude through third-party vendors, batch a p i use, realtime versus batch tradeoffs. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Thinking: adaptive and extended thinking, effort, fast mode, and what they cost. Prompt caching: what is cached, T T L s, minimums, prices and how to check a hit. Batch versus realtime: when each fits, and how batches work. Third-party platforms: Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud, Microsoft Foundry. A P I (application programming interface) errors and retries: the status codes, rate limits, backoff and request I Ds.

1.title: Case Check-In: Tidewater's Costly Answers
1.text: Our running case is Tidewater Insurance. Tidewater's Costly Answers. The claims assistant answers hard coverage questions well, but the monthly bill is high and some answers are slow. Most requests are simple lookups; a few need real reasoning. The team wants to spend reasoning only where it pays.

1.title: Thinking, Effort and Fast Mode
1.text: Thinking, Effort and Fast Mode. Adaptive thinking. What it does: The model decides how much to think, steered by effort. Notes: The mode on current models; no thinking field needed. Extended thinking. What it does: A fixed reasoning budget (budget tokens). Notes: Older manual mode; rejected with a four hundred error on current models, so use adaptive thinking. Effort (output config.effort). What it does: low, medium, high, xhigh, max: how thorough and how many tokens. Notes: A behavioral signal, not a hard budget; lower effort equals faster and cheaper for routine work.

1.title: Thinking, Effort and Fast Mode, continued
1.text: Thinking, Effort and Fast Mode, continued. Fast mode (speed: "fast"). What it does: Faster output (up to about two point five times) at premium pricing. Notes: For latency-critical work on supported models.

1.title: Thinking, Effort and Fast Mode, continued
1.text: Thinking, Effort and Fast Mode, continued. The figure shows this: Choosing reasoning: lower effort for routine work, higher effort for hard problems; thinking is billed as output and counts toward max tokens; fast mode buys speed at a premium. Thinking tokens are billed as output tokens and count toward max tokens, even if the text is not shown. Thinking blocks carry a signature and the text is a summary, not the raw reasoning.

1.title: Thinking, Effort and Fast Mode, continued
1.text: Thinking, Effort and Fast Mode, continued. Higher effort raises quality, latency and cost; step down when evals show quality holds, step up when they do not (Module eight). Exam tip: "Reduce cost and latency on simple requests" to lower effort (or a smaller model); "reasoning quality too low on hard cases" to higher effort or a stronger model, checked with evals.

1.title: Prompt Caching
1.text: Prompt Caching. Caching lets the A P I reuse the processed prefix of a prompt across requests, which cuts cost and latency for repeated content such as a long system prompt, policy text or tool definitions.

1.title: Prompt Caching, continued
1.text: Prompt Caching, continued. The figure shows this: Caching: put stable content first and mark a breakpoint; later requests with the same prefix read from the cache.

1.title: Prompt Caching, continued
1.text: Prompt Caching, continued. How. Automatic caching (one top-level cache control; the breakpoint moves forward) or explicit breakpoints on content blocks (up to four). What is cached. The full prefix, in order: tools, then system, then messages. A change earlier in the prefix invalidates what follows. Lifetime. five minutes by default (refreshed on each hit); one hour optionally at a higher write price. Price. Cache write about one point two five times the base input price (five minutes) or two times (one hour); cache read about zero point one times (even less on some models).

1.title: Prompt Caching, continued
1.text: Prompt Caching, continued. Minimum size. A minimum prompt length applies (for example five hundred twelve tokens on current models); shorter prompts are not cached, with no error. Check it. The response usage shows cache creation input tokens and cache read input tokens. Design rule: stable text first, volatile text last. A timestamp or user name at the top of the prompt breaks the cache on every call. Caching pays off when the same prefix is reused several times within the lifetime; a one-off prompt only pays the write cost.

1.title: Prompt Caching, continued
1.text: Prompt Caching, continued. Cached input tokens are not counted against the input tokens per minute rate limit the way uncached ones are. Current documentation: minimums, multipliers (read zero point one times, zero point zero five times on Opus five point five and Sonnet five point five, zero point zero two five times on Fable five point one) and T T L options. As of eight November two thousand twenty-six.

1.title: Realtime Versus Batch
1.text: Realtime Versus Batch. Response. Realtime (Messages A P I): Immediate (seconds). Message Batches A P I: Asynchronous: most finish within about an hour, up to twenty-four hours, no latency guarantee. Price. Realtime (Messages A P I): Standard. Message Batches A P I: fifty percent lower. Use for. Realtime (Messages A P I): Chat, interactive tools, blocking steps. Message Batches A P I: Non-urgent bulk work: overnight reports, evaluations, bulk classification. Mechanics. Realtime (Messages A P I): One call, one answer. Message Batches A P I: Create the batch, poll its status, read results by custom id (a batch holds up to one hundred thousand requests or two hundred fifty-six megabytes; results stay available about twenty-nine days). Limits. Realtime (Messages A P I): Tool loops possible in your code. Message Batches A P I: Each request is one model call: no tool round trip inside a request.

1.title: Realtime Versus Batch, continued
1.text: Realtime Versus Batch, continued. The figure shows this: Realtime when someone waits; batch when the work can wait and cost matters. Exam tip: Tens of thousands of archived records, results not needed for days, cost is the concern to Message Batches A P I. Parallel realtime calls do not lower the per-token price, and a smaller model chosen only for price ignores quality.

1.title: Third-Party Platforms
1.text: Third-Party Platforms. Claude is also available through Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud (Claude models on Google Cloud), Microsoft Foundry and Claude Platform on A W S. Why use them: your existing cloud contract, billing, identity (I A M) and data-residency controls.

1.title: Third-Party Platforms, continued
1.text: Third-Party Platforms, continued. Model I Ds. Differ by platform (for example anthropic.claude-opus-five to five on Bedrock; the Claude A P I I D on Google Cloud and Foundry). Auth. The cloud provider's identity (I A M roles, service accounts), not an Anthropic A P I key. S D K s (software development kit). The client S D K s have platform-specific clients with the same request shape. Features. Availability can lag or differ (for example images as base sixty-four only on Bedrock); check the platform page. Lifecycle. Partner platforms set their own retirement dates.

1.title: Third-Party Platforms, continued
1.text: Third-Party Platforms, continued. Choose a platform from the requirements (Module one): existing cloud commitment, residency, I A M integration. Use the first-party A P I when you need the newest features first.

1.title: API Errors and Retries
1.text: A P I Errors and Retries. The figure shows this: Fix the request for four X X errors; retry with backoff for four hundred twenty-nine, five X X and overloaded; honor retry-after.

1.title: API Errors and Retries, continued
1.text: A P I Errors and Retries, continued. four hundred invalid request. Meaning: Malformed request (bad parameter, unsupported combination). Action: Fix the request; do not retry unchanged. four hundred one or four hundred three. Meaning: Bad key or no permission. Action: Fix credentials or access. four hundred four or four hundred thirteen. Meaning: Not found or request too large. Action: Fix the path or reduce the request. four hundred twenty-nine rate limit. Meaning: Too many requests or tokens. Action: Back off, honor retry-after, reduce concurrency. five hundred or five hundred four or overloaded. Meaning: Server-side or transient. Action: Retry with exponential backoff.

2.title: API Errors and Retries, continued
2.text: A P I Errors and Retries, continued. Rate limits are measured in requests per minute, input tokens per minute and output tokens per minute, with a token-bucket that refills continuously; sharp increases in traffic can trigger acceleration limits, so ramp up gradually. The official S D K s retry transient errors twice by default with exponential backoff; tune the retry count and timeouts. Always log the request-id; an error can also arrive inside a stream (Module two). Exam tip: four X X: fix the request. four hundred twenty-nine: back off and honor retry-after. five X X or overloaded: retry with exponential backoff.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Thinking: Adaptive by default; manual budget tokens mode rejected on current models. Effort: low, medium, high, xhigh, max; lower equals cheaper and faster. Fast mode: speed: "fast": faster output at premium price. Caching: Stable prefix first; five min (or one h); write about one point two five times, read about zero point one times; minimum size. Batch: fifty percent cheaper; up to twenty-four h; custom id; poll; no mid-request tool loop. Realtime versus batch: Someone waits to realtime; can wait and cost matters to batch. Platforms: Bedrock, Google Cloud, Foundry, Claude Platform on A W S: cloud I A M, different I Ds and features. Errors: four X X fix the request; four hundred twenty-nine back off and honor retry-after; five X X or overloaded retry with exponential backoff.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Tidewater wants to re-tag eighty thousand archived claim emails for a quarterly audit that is due in a week; cost is the main concern and nobody waits on individual results. What fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Latency-tolerant bulk work at lower cost is what batches are for; parallel realtime calls do not cut the per-token price.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. The assistant sends the same forty-page policy text with every question, and requests are slow and costly. What is the best change? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. A stable prefix with a cache breakpoint is reused at a fraction of the cost and latency.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. A developer put the current time in the first line of the system prompt, and the cache hit rate is zero. Why? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Any change early in the prefix invalidates the cache; volatile text must come last.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. How can a developer verify that a request used the cache? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. The usage fields report cache writes and reads.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. A prompt marked for caching is shorter than the model's minimum cacheable length. What happens? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Prompts below the minimum are not cached, silently.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. A request returns H T T P four hundred twenty-nine with a retry-after header. What should the client do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. A rate limit calls for waiting, backoff and fewer concurrent calls.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. A request returns four hundred because of an unsupported parameter combination. What is the right response? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Client errors need a corrected request, not a retry.

2.title: Practice Question 8
2.text: Question eight. A company already runs on a cloud provider and needs Claude under its existing I A M and billing. What should it consider? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Claude is offered through major clouds with the cloud's identity and billing; I Ds and feature availability differ.

2.title: Practice Question 9
2.text: Question nine. Simple lookups and hard coverage questions use the same high-effort setting, so costs are high. What is a sound improvement? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Reasoning should be spent where it improves results, and evals confirm the quality holds.

2.title: Practice Question 10
2.text: Question ten. A developer sets a fixed budget tokens for thinking on a current model and gets a four hundred error. What is the likely cause? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Current models use adaptive thinking; the manual budget mode is rejected.

2.title: Practice Question 11
2.text: Question eleven. Select two. Which two statements about prompt caching are correct? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and C. The prefix must match, and reads are priced well below normal input; entries expire after their lifetime.

2.title: Practice Question 12
2.text: Question twelve. Select two. Which two are appropriate for the Message Batches A P I? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and E. Batches suit non-urgent bulk jobs; anything a person or a loop waits on needs realtime.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all twelve answers. Question one: C. Question two: C. Question three: C. Question four: D. Question five: A. Question six: B. Question seven: A. Question eight: C. Question nine: C. Question ten: D. Question eleven: B and C. Question twelve: B and E. In the next module, we continue the course.
